title: Remembering a Word Nobody Said
scopeNote: This keeps the studied lists with labelled sources and all three judgements at test, because the point is that the three come apart. The third list, the fuller source-monitoring analysis separating the two kinds of error, and the treatment of what warning people in advance does stay in the longer version.
summary: Two lists are read by two named people, each built so that every word points at one word that never appears. At test the learner judges ten words three ways, and the words they are surest about include one that was never on the screen.
learningObjectives: Describe how converging associates produce recognition of a word that was never presented.
Distinguish a recognition judgement, a confidence judgement and a source judgement.
Explain why confidence is not a measure of accuracy.
Explain why being able to name a source is not proof that something came from there.
Recognise that this demonstrates one specific mechanism rather than general unreliability of memory.
interactionTypes: a studied sequence of twenty words with named sources
three separate judgements per test word, each withheld until the previous is answered
a test set including unrelated words so a yes bias would be visible
feedback that names the learner's own false memories back to them
a full table of every word, what it really was, and what the learner said
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Every judgement is scored in the browser and is gone when the page is closed.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with every judgement a labelled button marked with a glyph and a hidden note as well as a colour. The display description names the reader and the word on every study item, so the study phase can be followed without seeing the panel. The study phase requires nothing to be pressed and nothing is timed out at test. The chart carries a description giving all three rates, and every word judged appears in a table with what it really was. Nothing flashes or moves; words change about once a second.
dataStatus: The learner's own judgements. The word lists were written for this activity rather than taken from a published set, so no published test material is reproduced and the lists are not calibrated; the caution says so and gives no rate anyone should expect.
simulationNotes: Two lists of ten words, each converging on a word that never appears, presented with one of two named readers. The test set is four studied words, four unrelated words and the two critical lures. The unrelated words are not padding: without them a high yes rate to the lures could simply be a bias towards saying yes, and the chart puts the two side by side so that comparison is available. All three judgements are kept because the finding is that they come apart: dropping the source question would leave an ordinary false-recognition demonstration, and dropping confidence would let a false memory look like a guess. Saying a word was not in the lists skips the other two questions, since confidence and source have nothing to attach to. Every outcome is handled in its own words, including not being caught at all, which is treated as an ordinary result rather than a failure.
readmeTopic: how a word that was never presented gets remembered confidently, and attributed to someone
